title: Routh I.Art.339 — TWO trajectories reach the same point at the same speed
abstract: Routh I.Art.339 — TWO trajectories reach the same point at the same speed — dynamic notebook
situation:
### The objects

| name | shape | given properties |
|---|---|---|
| `obj0` | `point` | `mass = 1e9`, `position = [0, 0, 0]` |
| `obj1` | `point` | `mass = 1`, `position = [1, 0, 0]`, `velocity = [0.1679448414712004, 1.1376706598234891, 0]` |
| `obj2` | `point` | `mass = 1e9`, `position = [0, 0, 0]` |
| `obj3` | `point` | `mass = 1`, `position = [1, 0, 0]`, `velocity = [0.8757322020879298, 0.745381184513149, 0]` |
| `obj4` | `point` | `mass = 1e9`, `position = [0, 0, 0]` |
| `obj5` | `point` | `mass = 1e-6`, `position = [1, 0, 0.0005]`, `velocity = [0.1679448414712004, 1.1376706598234891, 0]` |
| `obj6` | `point` | `mass = 1e-6`, `position = [1, 0, -0.0005]`, `velocity = [0.8757322020879298, 0.745381184513149, 0]` |

Each row is one rigid body. The simulator computes each body's inertia tensor from its shape; you never type an inertia tensor in.

### The shapes, and the inertia each implies

**`point`** — a massive point: it has mass but no size and no inertia. `I = 0`. A point cannot store rotational energy, so no torque turns it. Used for anchors, for planets whose size does not matter, and for charges. A `point` with `inverse_mass = 0` is the standard way to bolt a mechanism to the world.

### What each property means

- **`mass`** — the body's mass, in kilograms. Setting it also sets `inverse_mass` to its reciprocal — the two are kept consistent, and the simulator carries the inverse because that is what the equations of motion actually use.
- **`position`** — the centre of mass, as `[x, y, z]` in metres.
- **`velocity`** — the centre-of-mass velocity, as `[vx, vy, vz]` in metres per second. Setting it sets the linear momentum to `m * v`; the momentum is what the state vector actually carries.

### The interactions

- **Mutual gravity is ON**, with `G = 1e-9`. Every pair of bodies attracts every other by `F = G m1 m2 / r^2`, softened at short range if `softening` is set.
- **Contact is OFF**. Nothing here is meant to touch anything else, so the rootfinder is not armed.
eom:
There are 7 bodies. Each obeys Newton's and Euler's equations, both of which are **second order**:

```
m_i * d2(x_i)/dt2 = F_grav_i

I_i * d(omega_i)/dt + omega_i x (I_i omega_i) = T_i
```

The `omega x (I omega)` term in Euler's equation is the gyroscopic term. It is what makes a tumbling body's spin axis wander even with no torque at all, and it is why rigid-body motion cannot be reduced to three independent rotations.

The forces on the right are:

- `F_grav_i = sum over j != i of G m_i m_j (x_j - x_i) / |x_j - x_i|^3` — the mutual attraction, softened at short range if `softening` is set
constraints:
**This model has no joints.** Nothing algebraic relates the coordinates, so the system is an ordinary differential equation rather than a differential-algebraic one, and it needs no Lagrange multipliers and no constraint Jacobian.

That does not mean nothing is conserved. Energy, linear momentum and angular momentum are still exact consequences of the equations of motion, and comparing them before and after a run is the honest way to judge the integration.
reduction:
**Sizing this particular problem.** There are 7 bodies, so the state vector `y` has

```
7 bodies x 13 numbers = 91 components
```

laid out as consecutive 13-number blocks in creation order, each holding position (3), linear momentum (3), orientation quaternion w-first (4), and angular momentum (3).

**What is handed to the Rust SUNDIALS translation.**

There are no algebraic constraints, so the whole of the mechanics above is one first-order system

```
dy/dt = f(t, y),   y in R^91
```

handed to the pure-Rust translation of **CVODE** in Adams-Moulton mode: a variable-order, variable-step explicit-family method for non-stiff problems. This is the default, and it is the right choice for orbits and for anything smooth.

The right-hand side `f` unpacks `y` into bodies, computes every force and torque, and packs the derivatives back in the same 13-per-body order.

steps.title: Set up the world
steps.explain:
The next cell sends these 4 commands to the simulator. Here is exactly what each one expects:

---

`set system.rtol = 1e-13` sets a property of the whole simulation rather than of one body. `rtol` is the integrator's relative error tolerance. Smaller is more accurate and slower. Joints that grip orientation impose a floor of `1e-6`, because the index-2 accuracy ceiling is real and asking for more produces convergence failures rather than better answers.

The value expected here is `1e-13`. A successful `set` prints nothing.

---

`set system.atol = 1e-15` sets a property of the whole simulation rather than of one body. `atol` is the integrator's absolute error tolerance, which is what governs components passing near zero, where a relative tolerance means nothing. Orientation joints impose a floor of `1e-8`.

The value expected here is `1e-15`. A successful `set` prints nothing.

---

`set system.softening = 0` sets a property of the whole simulation rather than of one body. `softening` is a length that softens the mutual gravity at short range, replacing `1/r^2` with `1/(r^2 + s^2)`. It stops the force blowing up when two bodies pass very close. Too small a value is nearly singular when surfaces touch.

The value expected here is `0`. A successful `set` prints nothing.

---

`set system.g_constant = 1e-9` sets a property of the whole simulation rather than of one body. `g_constant` is the gravitational constant `G` used for the mutual attraction between every pair of bodies, `F = G m1 m2 / r^2`. **Its default is 1, not 0**, which catches people out: bodies rattling in a box also attract each other unless you say otherwise. Set it to 0 for a mechanism or a collision experiment; set it to a real value for an orbit.

The value expected here is `1e-9`. A successful `set` prints nothing.
steps.code:
sim.do("set system.rtol = 1e-13")
sim.do("set system.atol = 1e-15")
sim.do("set system.softening = 0")
sim.do("set system.g_constant = 1e-9")

`run 2.16112` advances the simulation by **2.16112 seconds of duration** — not to absolute time 2.16112. This trips people up: `run 1.7` followed by `run 2.89` leaves you at t = 4.59, not at 2.89. The form is `RUN <duration> [STEPS <n>]`.

`steps 2` asks for the result to be reported at 2 equally spaced points across that interval. It does not set the integrator's internal step size — SUNDIALS chooses that itself from the error tolerances, and takes as many internal steps between reports as accuracy demands.

This is the cell that actually integrates, so it is the slow one. It prints the time reached and how many internal solver steps were needed.

`scene create` opens the graphical scene window. It starts a small HTTP and WebSocket server — hand-rolled on `std::net`, with no web framework — and prints the address to open in a browser. The window shows the bodies as wireframes, with a readout of energy, momentum and angular momentum that updates live.

The window evolves its **own copy** of the system. Stepping in the notebook does not move the window, and playing the window does not move the notebook. That isolation is deliberate.

If the environment variable `POSIM_NO_BROWSER` is set, the address is printed but no browser is launched — which is what happens when this notebook is run non-interactively.

discussion:
**What the cells above actually established.**

- `energy` was printed. Compare the value before the run with the value after it. For a closed system with no dissipation they should agree to near machine precision, and the size of the disagreement is the honest measure of the integration — not a number to be talked around.

**How to judge a number here.** A disagreement with theory is only a defect if it fails to shrink when you ask for more accuracy. Tighten `system.rtol` and `system.atol` and re-run: a discretisation error converges, and a bug does not. The one place this does not apply is a model with orientation-gripping joints, where `rtol` is floored at `1e-6` and tightening past it buys nothing.

**The full note from the example this notebook pairs with**, which sets out why it was built this way:

Routh I.Art.339 — TWO trajectories reach the same point at the same speed
— dynamic notebook

E. J. Routh, "A Treatise on Dynamics of a Particle" (Cambridge, 1898),
Part I, Art. 339: "To project a particle with a given velocity V from a
given point P so that it shall pass through another given point Q."

THE CONSTRUCTION. The centre of force S occupies one focus. Energy fixes the
major axis and nothing else (Art. 335): V^2 = mu*(2/R - 1/a). The OTHER
focus H is then pinned by the focal property SP + PH = 2a, so

|PH| = 2a - r1        and        |QH| = 2a - r2

H lies on two circles, about P and about Q. Two circles meet in TWO points,
so there are exactly TWO orbits of that speed from P to Q — the flat one and
the lofted one. They merge only at maximum range, where the circles touch.
This is the same two-solution structure as the projectile directrix
construction of Art. 159, and the reason a target is reachable by two paths.

THE NUMBERS. mu = 1 (a heavy primary at the origin with G*M_total = 1),
P = (1, 0) with r1 = 1, Q = (0, 1.6) with r2 = 1.6, speed V = 1.15. Then

a  = 1 / (2/r1 - V^2/mu) = 1.476014760147601
|PH| = 2a - r1 = 1.952029520295202
|QH| = 2a - r2 = 1.352029520295202
|PQ| = 1.886796226411321        (so the circles genuinely intersect)

H1 = ( 1.3119022576347596,  1.9269499811324258)
H2 = (-0.8687661408803334,  0.5640322320604925)

The launch direction at P is the tangent, which by the reflection property
bisects the angle between PS and PH: t_hat = normalize(unit(PH) - unit(PS)).
That gives, for the two foci and a common counter-clockwise sense,

orbit A:  v = (0.1679448414712004, 1.1376706598234891, 0)
orbit B:  v = (0.8757322020879298, 0.745381184513149,  0)

Both have |v| = 1.15 exactly and the same semi-major axis. Orbit A runs
DIRECT to Q, arriving at t = 2.16112. Orbit B leaves on a shallower tangent,
sweeps most of the way round the primary, and arrives at the same point at
t = 8.89752 -- the period being 2*pi*sqrt(a^3/mu) = 11.267197811607677.
Two speeds equal, two paths utterly different, one target.

HOW THE CELLS CHECK IT. Each orbit is flown ALONE, so nothing perturbs it,
and the printed value is its distance from Q at the predicted instant. Both
read ~1e-6, which is the resolution of the arrival time quoted above rather
than any error in the integration.

WHAT YOU WATCH: two particles leave the same point at the same speed. One
cuts straight across to the target; the other swings the long way around the
primary and arrives at exactly the same place. In the scene the two are given
mass 1e-6 and are separated by 0.001 in z -- purely so they are two distinct
bodies rather than one singular pair; at that mass their mutual attraction is
~1e-15 of the primary's pull and changes nothing you can see.
